prompt: In Microsoft's comparison of AKS Automatic and Standard, what does a feature marked preconfigured mean?
hint: Three words sort every feature; this is the strictest.

choices.text: Set up for you when the cluster is created, and yours to change afterwards
choices.why: That is the word default, such as the planned maintenance window.

choices.text: On, with no way to switch it off or change its settings
choices.why: Right. The upgrade channel stable and the Standard tier are two of them on Automatic.

choices.text: Available on the cluster but off until you configure it
choices.why: That is optional, the state of most features on Standard.

choices.text: Present on Automatic and absent from Standard altogether
choices.why: Most preconfigured features exist on Standard as options; what differs is whether you may change them.

prompt: Lesson 11's system pool was three Standard_D4s_v5 in your node resource group. On an Automatic cluster with managed system node pools, where do the system nodes run?
hint: Whose subscription, and whose bill.

choices.text: In your node resource group, billed to you as before
choices.why: That was Standard. Managed system node pools move them out of your subscription.

choices.text: In your subscription, inside a locked resource group you cannot list
choices.why: The node resource group is locked, but it holds your nodes; the system nodes are not in your subscription.

choices.text: On the API server's machines, paid for by the tier
choices.why: They are nodes of their own, apart from the control plane, and the documentation ties their cost to no tier.

choices.text: In AKS's own subscriptions, and not charged to yours at all
choices.why: Right. AKS creates, scales and upgrades them there, and you track no quota for them.

prompt: Automatic's pod readiness SLA says 99.9% of qualifying pod readiness operations complete within five minutes. In a month with 5,000 such operations, how many may take longer without the promise being broken?
hint: 0.1% of the operations.

prompt: Which of these is preconfigured on an Automatic cluster, so that you cannot change it?
hint: Three are defaults or options; one is locked.

choices.text: The managed virtual network on Azure CNI Overlay with Cilium
choices.why: A default: a virtual network of your own is the option.

choices.text: The cluster upgrade channel, stable, following minor version N-1
choices.why: Right. The cluster follows the latest patch of N-1 and you cannot pick another channel.

choices.text: A planned maintenance window for the upgrades
choices.why: A default you may set and change, which is how you decide when the channel's upgrades start.

choices.text: Managed Prometheus collecting the cluster's metrics
choices.why: A default when the cluster is created from the CLI or the portal, not a locked setting.

prompt: slip.bicep compiled with tier: 'Free' and name: 'automatic' and warned only about the string 'true'. What does the silence about the tier tell Ana?
hint: What did the compiler have to compare the value against?

choices.text: That an Automatic cluster may run on the Free tier
choices.why: The documentation says the tier is preconfigured as Standard; the compiler knows nothing of that rule.

choices.text: That sku.tier takes any string, and the service decides
choices.why: Right. A wider type means a silent compile; whether Azure refuses or corrects it is only known on a subscription.

choices.text: That Bicep rewrote Free to Standard in the template it wrote
choices.why: The compiler copies the value as written; it never changes a property's value.

choices.text: That the deployment will fail with the same BCP036 warning
choices.why: BCP036 was about the boolean, and a deployment is answered by Resource Manager, not by the compiler.

prompt: What does node auto-provisioning read to decide which virtual machine size to create?
hint: It starts from the pods, not from a pool.

choices.text: The vmSize of the pool it has been asked to grow
choices.why: That is the cluster autoscaler's input; NAP has no fixed size to grow.

choices.text: The requests of the pods the scheduler left Pending
choices.why: Right. The pending pods' requests, intersected with what the NodePools allow.

choices.text: The CPU the running nodes used over the last hour
choices.why: Usage is not what scheduling or NAP counts; requests are.

choices.text: A size chosen once when the cluster was created
choices.why: There is no such size on Automatic; that is what the NodePool's range replaces.

prompt: Match each object to what it says.
hint: Two you write, one NAP writes, and one that adds a type to the API server.

pairs.right: Which machines may be created, and when they may be removed
The Azure half of a node: image family, OS disk, maxPods
NAP's record of one node it asked Azure for
Adds a new kind of object to the API server

right_distractors: The scale set behind a pool of one fixed size

prompt: A NodePool owns 12 nodes and has one budget of nodes: "30%". One node is already being deleted and none is unready. How many more nodes may Karpenter disrupt now?
hint: The percentage of the node count, rounded up, minus the nodes deleting and the nodes not ready.

prompt: The first dry run of slips.yaml named two problems and said some validation rules were not checked. Why did the agentpool key only show up on the second run?
hint: Read the last line of the first answer.

choices.text: The API server reports at most two errors for any one object
choices.why: It reported every structural error it found; the count was a coincidence of the slips.

choices.text: kubectl stops reading the file at the first field refused
choices.why: kubectl sends the whole object; the server refused two fields far apart in it.

choices.text: The key is allowed until a node exists to carry the label
choices.why: It was refused on the second run with no node anywhere, so the rule does not wait for nodes.

choices.text: Expression rules run only once the structural checks pass
choices.why: Right. The value list and the pattern failed first, so the CEL rule on label domains was skipped until they passed.

prompt: A NodePool requires karpenter.azure.com/sku-family In [Dpls_v6], and the API server accepts it. On AKS, what happens to a pod that only this pool could serve?
hint: Accepted by the definition is not the same as matching a machine.

choices.text: NAP creates a Dpls_v6 machine, since that series exists
choices.why: Dpls_v6 is a series, matched by the sku-series key; no machine reports it as its family.

choices.text: It stays Pending, because no machine reports that family
choices.why: Right. The CRD checks that the key is allowed, not that its values name anything.

choices.text: NAP reads the first letter and creates a D-series machine
choices.why: Values are compared whole; nothing in Karpenter guesses at a family from a series.

choices.text: Karpenter marks the pool invalid and stops scaling the cluster
choices.why: The pool is valid as far as any check goes; it simply matches nothing.

prompt: On an Automatic cluster, what can you change about the deployment safeguards?
hint: One thing, and it is about where they apply.

choices.text: Their level, from Enforce down to Warn
choices.why: That is the one change Automatic refuses; it is possible on Standard.

choices.text: Which of the rules are switched on
choices.why: The safeguards are all or nothing, on every SKU.

choices.text: Which namespaces they leave alone
choices.why: Right. Excluding a namespace is the only way round them on Automatic.

choices.text: The default requests the mutator writes
choices.why: 500m and 2048Mi are fixed in the mutator; you avoid them by writing your own requests.

prompt: kind accepted hurried.yaml and its pod ran. Which QoS class did Kubernetes give it, and why?
hint: The class is computed from the resources section.

choices.text: Burstable, because it declared a port but no limits
choices.why: Burstable needs at least one request or limit; a port has nothing to do with the class.

choices.text: BestEffort, because no container asked for or was limited to anything
choices.why: Right. No requests and no limits is the definition of BestEffort, the first class evicted under pressure.

choices.text: Guaranteed, because nothing else competed with it on the node it ran on
choices.why: Guaranteed needs requests equal to limits on every container; the neighbours do not count.

choices.text: None: a class is assigned by the safeguards, which kind lacks
choices.why: The class is Kubernetes's own, and the transcript printed it.

prompt: With the tag latest and no pull policy in the manifest, the API server defaults imagePullPolicy to ___.
hint: The dry run printed it.

prompt: Six replicas of a container with no resources section are created on an Automatic cluster. After the mutator, how many GiB of memory do they request in all?
hint: The mutator's default memory request, times the replicas.

prompt: Which of these does the Enforce level refuse rather than mutate? Choose all that apply.
hint: Two rules have a mutator; the others can only say no.

choices.text: A container with no liveness probe
choices.why: The probes rule has no mutator: it refuses, naming the missing probe.

choices.text: The image shop:latest
choices.why: Refused, with the message asking for an explicit, versioned tag.

choices.text: A container with no resource requests
choices.why: Mutated: the mutator writes 500m and 2048Mi as requests and limits.

choices.text: Three replicas with no anti-affinity or spread constraint
choices.why: Mutated: anti-affinity and a topology spread constraint are added.

choices.text: kubectl taint on one node
choices.why: Refused: nodes are tainted by pool, never one at a time.

prompt: Why can a development cluster on Automatic not save money by being stopped every evening?
hint: One of the preconfigured pieces forbids it.

choices.text: Stopping is refused on every Standard-tier cluster
choices.why: A Standard cluster on the base SKU can be stopped; the tier is not the reason.

choices.text: The managed system nodes would keep running and billing
choices.why: Their machines are not charged to your subscription, stopped or not.

choices.text: Node auto-provisioning refuses the stop operation outright
choices.why: Right. It is on the documentation's list of NAP's limitations, and NAP is preconfigured.

choices.text: The pod readiness SLA requires the cluster to be running
choices.why: An SLA is a promise about the service, and it never forbids an operation.

prompt: The shop wants the Dapr extension on AKS, to bring lesson 9's sidecars into a cluster. What does that decide?
hint: Read the documentation's list of unsupported extensions.

choices.text: Automatic, with Dapr's namespace excluded from the safeguards
choices.why: Exclusion is about policy; the extension itself is not supported on Automatic.

choices.text: Standard: Automatic does not support that extension
choices.why: Right. Dapr and Azure Machine Learning are the two extensions the documentation lists as unsupported.

choices.text: Automatic, since KEDA comes preconfigured and Dapr builds on it
choices.why: Dapr does not build on KEDA, and KEDA being on says nothing about the extension.

choices.text: Either, provided the cluster is in brazilsouth
choices.why: The region decides whether Automatic exists there, not which extensions it runs.

prompt: Put the steps of moving shop-auto from Automatic to Standard in order.
hint: The cluster needs somewhere to run its system pods before it stops being Automatic.
items: Add a system node pool of your own, in System mode
Update the cluster's SKU to base
Check with az aks show that the SKU is now base
List the node pools and find your system pool among them
trap: The pool comes first: a Standard cluster runs its system pods on your machines, and there must be some.

prompt: On Automatic, what decides the size, and so the price, of the machines the shop's pods land on?
hint: Where the vmSize of lesson 11 went.

choices.text: The vmSize of a user pool called apps
choices.why: There is no such pool on Automatic; NAP creates nodes with no pool size behind them.

choices.text: The node size that comes with the Standard tier
choices.why: The tier is about the control plane's promise; it fixes no node size.

choices.text: What each container requests, within the NodePools' range
choices.why: Right. NAP sizes machines from requests, so whoever writes the Deployment chooses the bill.

choices.text: What the pods used last week, as the image cleaner reports it
choices.why: The image cleaner removes unused images; it measures nothing about pods.

prompt: Which of these teams has a reason to choose Standard over Automatic?
hint: Look for a need that no preconfigured setting can meet.

choices.text: Three developers who want no node pools or channels to own
choices.why: That is the team Automatic is for.

choices.text: A shop in brazilsouth that wants an uptime SLA on the API server
choices.why: brazilsouth is on the list of regions, and the SLA comes preconfigured.

choices.text: A team that needs one Kubernetes version for two years
choices.why: Right. Long-term support needs the Premium tier, and Automatic is preconfigured on Standard.

choices.text: A team that wants node sizes chosen from what its pods request
choices.why: That is node auto-provisioning, which Automatic gives you.

prompt: Which of these slips did something in this lesson's lab catch before anything was stored? Choose all that apply.
hint: Two checkers ran: the Bicep compiler and the API server with the NodePool CRD.

choices.text: enabled: 'true' in automatic.bicep
choices.why: BCP036: the property expected a boolean.

choices.text: tier: 'Free' in automatic.bicep
choices.why: It compiled in silence: the type of sku.tier takes any string.

choices.text: consolidationPolicy: WhenUnderutilized in a NodePool
choices.why: The CRD lists the three values it supports, and this is not one.

choices.text: sku-family: Dpls_v6 in a NodePool
choices.why: Accepted: the key is allowed, and its values are not checked.

choices.text: a budget of nodes: "120%"
choices.why: The CRD's pattern allows at most 100%.

choices.text: image: shop:latest in a pod
choices.why: kind stored it and ran it; only a safeguard would have refused it.

prompt: Gatekeeper fails open. Which of these can therefore happen on an Automatic cluster?
hint: Fails open means: when in doubt, admit.

choices.text: A compliant Deployment refused because the webhook was slow
choices.why: That would be failing closed, which Gatekeeper avoids so a slow policy service blocks nothing.

choices.text: Every deployment held until the policy service answers again
choices.why: Holding requests is the opposite of failing open.

choices.text: A Deployment with no probes, admitted while nobody was checking
choices.why: Right. The check is skipped and the object admitted, so a noncompliant workload can be in the cluster.

choices.text: The mutator writing requests while the probe rule alone is skipped
choices.why: Mutation and validation are both admission calls; an unanswered webhook skips the check, not half of it.

prompt: The shop's NodePool has limits of cpu: "64". If every node NAP creates for it has 16 vCPUs, how many such nodes can the pool hold at once?
hint: The limit counts all the pool's nodes together.

prompt: A pod that consolidation must leave where it is carries the annotation karpenter.sh/___: "true".
hint: Three words joined by hyphens.
